terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where try.js starts your API on a free port and sends it a few requests.

tasks.title: Create a workshop
tasks.description:
Add `POST /workshops` to `createApp` in `src/app.js`. It reads a JSON body like `{ "title": "Throwing bowls", "day": "fri", "seats": 6, "priceCents": 4500 }` and:

- saves the workshop with `store.create(...)`, which picks the id
- saves **only** `title`, `day`, `seats` and `priceCents`; an `id` or any other field in the body is left out (`FIELDS` in `src/validate.js` lists the four)
- answers `201` with the saved workshop and a `location` header that points at it, such as `/workshops/6`

Validation comes in the next two tasks. The check posts workshops, reads them back and posts one with fields that must not be saved.
nextSteps: Run `node try.js` and look at the first answer: Express has no route for it yet.
Turn on JSON body parsing for the app, before the routes.
Add the POST route, keep only the four fields and save them.
Answer 201 with the location header, then run `node try.js` again.
hints: Express does not read request bodies by itself. `req.body` stays `undefined` until a middleware fills it.
`app.use(express.json())` reads JSON bodies into `req.body`. To keep only some fields, build a new object from `FIELDS`.

tasks.title: Check what was sent
tasks.description:
Implement `validateWorkshop(body)` in `src/validate.js`. It returns the names of the fields that are missing or wrong, in the order `title`, `day`, `seats`, `priceCents`, and `[]` when the workshop is fine:

- `title`: text that is not empty once spaces are trimmed, at most 80 characters
- `day`: one of `DAYS`
- `seats`: a whole number from 1 to 20
- `priceCents`: a whole number, 0 or more

A body that is not an object at all (`undefined`, `null`, an array, a string) gets all four names. Other fields do not matter here.

The check calls your function with good workshops, values on both sides of each limit, and bodies that are not workshops.
nextSteps: First handle a body that is not a plain object.
Write one small test per field.
Return the fields whose test fails, in the order of `FIELDS`.
Press Check: it calls the function directly.
hints: `typeof` is not enough on its own: it says `"object"` for `null` and for arrays too.
`Number.isInteger` is false for `2.5`, for `'6'` and for `NaN`, which covers most of what a number rule needs.

`if (typeof body !== 'object' || body === null || Array.isArray(body)) return [...FIELDS]`, then keep one test per field in an object `rules` and return `FIELDS.filter((field) => !rules[field](body[field]))`.

tasks.title: Refuse a bad workshop
tasks.description:
Use `validateWorkshop` in `POST /workshops`. When it finds problems:

- answer `400` with `{ "error": { "code": "validation_failed", "message": "...", "fields": [...] } }`, where `fields` is the list `validateWorkshop` returned
- save nothing

A POST with no JSON body at all leaves `req.body` as `undefined`, and must get the same 400, not a crash. Good workshops are still created as before.

The check posts workshops with wrong fields, no body and a list, then checks that nothing was saved.
nextSteps: Call `validateWorkshop` with the body at the start of the route.
When the list is not empty, answer 400 and stop.
Make sure the store only sees bodies that passed.
Run `node try.js` and look at the last two answers.
hints: The body is the one part of a request you cannot trust. Check it before anything else uses it.
The route has two endings now. Return the 400 so the code after it does not run.
`const problems = validateWorkshop(req.body)`, then `if (problems.length > 0) return res.status(400).json({ error: { code: 'validation_failed', message, fields: problems } })`.
